name: libmagic
why: The engine behind file(1) uses a huge magic-number database that is a fun window into how file formats are identified.

brief.what_it_is: libmagic is the library behind the Unix file(1) command, which identifies what kind of data a file holds by reading its contents rather than trusting its name. It takes a file (or a buffer of bytes) and a compiled magic database, and returns a human-readable description such as the type or MIME type. The file command is the thin front end; the library lets other programs do the same identification without forking and exec'ing file. One example given is the Python file module, which wraps it.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames it around the idea that command-line systems do not rely on filename extensions and instead inspect the actual contents, which is more reliable but needs some I/O. The README says the library split exists so that 3rd party programs can identify file types without having to fork() and exec() file.
brief.how_it_works: The engine checks the file against a database of 'magic numbers' kept in /etc/magic and a Magdir directory of pieces, parsed by apprentice.c. Tests run in stages: fsmagic.c checks filesystem info first, softmagic.c applies the magic-file rules, and ascmagic.c applies hardwired checks as the last stage. Compressed files can be looked inside via compress.c, though that is compiled out on the Amiga runtimes because they cannot spawn external decompressors.

brief.install_notes: The homepage points to source tarballs at ftp://ftp.astron.com/pub/file/ and says file ships with most Linux distributions and BSDs, so most users never build it. The GitHub README points to an INSTALL file for building from source; I did not read it. Building from a git checkout needs autoreconf -i before configure, per the Amiga section. Compiling the magic database needs no special hardware or accounts. Amiga cross-builds use Docker images (sacredbanana/amiga-compiler) and a list of configure flags that the README covers at length.
brief.standout: The database is the interesting part: the README says the maintainer accepts new magic entries in magic(5) format, and the Magdir guidelines are strict, requiring unique matches of at least 32 bits and rejecting matches of 16 bits or fewer. The project also dates to August 1987, when Ian Darwin's first RCS commit was made, after the original Bell Labs file was unavailable in source form.
brief.status: maintained. The GitHub README is an RCS-tagged file dated 2026/10/03, the README describes Release 5.x with a named maintainer (Christos Zoulas), there is an active CI workflow for Amiga packaging that runs on every push to master, and the homepage lists ongoing mailing-list release announcements. I did not see a release date or last-commit date directly.
brief.caveats: Much of the GitHub README is about AmigaOS and MorphOS cross-compilation, with several runtimes not supported (newlib on m68k, clib2 and newlib on AmigaOS 4). Compressed-file inspection via external decompressors is compiled out on those platforms. The README's licensing is described as 'copyright but distributable' and points to a COPYING file, which I did not read. The homepage's FreshMeat link is marked as not working. The README also carries an old 'Send cash first!' joke about phone support, which is not a real policy.
quotes: It knows the 'magic number' of several thousands of file types.
Unlike most GUI systems, command-line *NIX systems - with this program leading the charge - don’t rely on filename extentions to tell you the type of a file, but look at the file’s actual contents.
Initial match is preferably at least 32 bits long, and is a _unique_ match
